# 1 Corinthians 15:30–58 — Verse-by-Verse Commentary Notes

---

## v. 30 — “And why do we endanger ourselves every hour?”

Paul applies the same logical argument from v. 29 to the apostles themselves: their constant risk-taking makes no sense if there is no resurrection. Ellicott notes the strong contrast between “them” in v. 29 and “we” here — Paul shifts from the practice of others to his own apostolic band. Their conduct would be “illogical if they did not believe in a resurrection.”

- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_corinthians/15.htm

Gill adds that Paul and his co-workers “continually expose ourselves to dangers, and are for Christ’s sake killed all the day long, are every moment liable to innumerable injuries, tortures and death; who in his senses would act such a part, if there is no resurrection of the dead?” Such people would be “of all men the most miserable” and also “of all men the most stupid.”

- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-corinthians-15.html

---

## v. 31 — “I face death every day, brothers, as surely as I boast about you in Christ Jesus our Lord.”

Ellicott renders the opening as “I protest by your boast which I have in Christ Jesus.” Paul’s converts are his “boasting” (cf. 2 Cor 9:3), and by the fact that they are his in the Lord, he makes the solemn assertion “I die daily.” Such a life — both in spiritual battles within his own soul and in ceaseless conflict with enemies around him — “was indeed a daily dying” (see 2 Cor 11:23–28).

- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_corinthians/15.htm

---

## v. 32 — “If I fought wild beasts in Ephesus for human motives, what did I gain? If the dead are not raised, ‘Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we die.’”

**Traditional reading:** Most commentators take “fought wild beasts” metaphorically — referring to fierce human opponents in Ephesus, not literal beasts in an arena, since Paul was a Roman citizen and would not have been subjected to such punishment, and he does not mention it in his list of sufferings in 2 Corinthians 11. Gill notes this as an instance of Paul’s daily danger. Paul then quotes Isaiah 22:13 — if there is no resurrection, the only logical lifestyle is hedonistic despair. The denial of resurrection leads directly to moral collapse.

- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-corinthians-15.html
- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_corinthians/15.htm

**Enduring Word** (David Guzik, charismatic/Pentecostal): This verse is part of Paul’s *reductio ad absurdum* — if there is no resurrection, even the apostles’ sacrifices are pointless. The Epicurean motto “let us eat and drink” is the natural endpoint of denying future bodily life.

- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-corinthians-15/

---

## v. 33 — “Do not be deceived: ‘Bad company corrupts good character.’”

**Traditional reading:** The quotation is an iambic trimeter from the Greek comic poet Menander (c. 322 BC), though it was likely a proverbial saying before him. The Greek *homiliai* can mean “conversations” (Vulgate: *colloquia mala*) or more broadly “companionships/intercourse” (RV). In context, the “bad company” are the deniers of the resurrection within the Corinthian church (the *tines* of v. 12). Their bad theology was leading to bad morals, and Paul warns the church not to be seduced by them.

- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_corinthians/15.htm
- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_corinthians/15-33.htm (Meyer’s NT Commentary via Bible Hub)

**John MacArthur (Baptist – gty.org):** *Homilia* (company) can also carry the connotation of a lecture or sermon. The Corinthians were both listening to wrong teaching and associating with evil people. “People who think wrongly invariably behave wrongly.” The heretical theology denying the resurrection “had corrupted good morals.” Hoping in the resurrection is an incentive to holiness; disbelieving it is an incentive to immorality.

- https://shop.gty.org/library/bibleqnas-library/QA0037/bad-company-corrupts-good-character
- https://www.gty.org/sermons/90-495/what-resurrection-means-for-you

**Ligonier (Reformed):** Paul’s warning is that bad company “inevitably and invariably” corrupts. Proverbs 12:26 provides the takeaway: “The righteous choose their friends carefully.”

- https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/discipleship-and-growth

---

## v. 34 — “Sober up as you ought, and stop sinning; for some of you are ignorant of God. I say this to your shame.”

**Traditional reading:** Ellicott notes the literal sense is “Awake to soberness in a righteous manner.” This is an urgent call to “arouse from the sleep of indulgence and of death.” The “some” who have “an ignorance regarding God” are those who call themselves Christians yet deny the resurrection. “To their shame” the Apostle speaks — it was a disgrace that to Christians Paul should have to vindicate the most fundamental truth of the Faith.

- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_corinthians/15.htm

**Meyer’s Commentary** notes that the aorist imperative *eknēpsate* (“sober up”) demands swift, instant realization of becoming sober, while *mē hamartanete* (“stop sinning”) requires continuous abstinence. The *tines* (certain ones) are those from v. 12 — their unbelief in the resurrection stems from *agnōsia theou* (ignorance of God). The church is disgraced that such people remain within it.

- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_corinthians/15-33.htm

---

## v. 35 — “But someone will ask, ‘How are the dead raised? With what kind of body will they come?’”

**Traditional reading:** Paul now turns from proving the *fact* of resurrection to answering objections about its *manner*. Ellicott outlines this as the beginning of a new section (vv. 35–58): “The Method and Principle of the Resurrection.” The two questions represent a sceptical challenge: “How are the dead raised?” (in what manner?) and “With what body do they come?” The second question sharpens the first — the objection is that a decomposed body cannot possibly be reassembled.

- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_corinthians/15.htm

Gill: Paul “proceeds to answer questions, and remove objections relating to the resurrection of the dead; which questions and objections … suppose the thing to be impossible and absurd.”

- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-corinthians-15.html

---

## v. 36 — “You fool! What you sow does not come to life unless it dies.”

Paul’s sharp “You fool!” (*aphron*) is not mere insult — it is the biblical term for one who fails to reason from God’s created order (cf. Ps 14:1). The seed analogy is his first answer: a seed placed in the ground undergoes a kind of “death” — it dissolves and ceases to be a seed — yet from that dissolution springs new life. The resurrection is not the reassembly of old particles but a divinely ordered transformation, just as a seed “dies” and then germinates into a plant far more glorious than itself.

- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_corinthians/15.htm

Gill: grain “first dies before it is quickened, and … does not rise up bare grain as it was sown, but in a different form and shape, with additional circumstances greatly to its advantage.”

- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-corinthians-15.html

**John Piper (Desiring God, Baptist/Reformed):** Paul “is not denying that it will be the same body. Instead, he is affirming that in the resurrection our bodies will be made better than the state they are now in.” Just as a plant is the same organism as the seed yet transformed, so “the same body we have now becomes our resurrected body.”

- https://www.desiringgod.org/articles/do-we-receive-the-same-body-we-had-on-earth-at-the-resurrection

---

## vv. 37–38 — “And what you sow is not the body that will be, but just a seed … But God gives it a body as He has designed…”

Paul stresses both discontinuity (the bare seed looks nothing like the mature plant) and continuity (God gives *to each kind of seed* its own appropriate body). The transformation is by God’s design and power, not by natural process alone. The resurrection body is both genuinely connected to the present body and surpassingly glorious.

- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_corinthians/15.htm

Piper notes on v. 38: “Paul is not teaching about evolution here, but he is showing how he takes God’s intimate involvement with creation for granted. Evidently, Paul cannot imagine that any natural process should be conceived of without God’s doing it.” God gives “to each and every seed its own body” — individual, not merely generic.

- https://www.desiringgod.org/solid-joys/the-marvel-of-creation

---

## v. 39 — “Not all flesh is the same: Men have one kind of flesh, animals another, birds another, and fish another.”

Paul expands the analogy: just as God has created different kinds of “flesh” suited to different creatures, He is fully able to create a resurrection “flesh” suited to the heavenly life. This answers the objection “with what kind of body?” — God has infinite variety at His disposal.

- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_corinthians/15.htm

Gill: “though all of it flesh, differs from each other; and so will the flesh of the body, in the resurrection, differ from the flesh it is now clothed with.”

- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-corinthians-15.html

---

## vv. 40–41 — “There are also heavenly bodies and earthly bodies … The sun has one degree of splendor, the moon another, and the stars another…”

Paul now illustrates from the heavens: just as there is a vast difference in “splendor” (*doxa*, glory) between the sun, moon, and stars — yet all are “bodies” — so the resurrection body will differ in glory from the present body. Gill clarifies: these similes show “not any difference there will be in risen bodies among themselves, but in risen bodies from what they now are.” The point is transformation, not gradations of reward (though some have seen an implication of differing glories among the resurrected).

- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-corinthians-15.html

---

## vv. 42–44 — The Four Contrasts: “What is sown is perishable; it is raised imperishable. It is sown in dishonor; it is raised in glory. It is sown in weakness; it is raised in power. It is sown a natural body; it is raised a spiritual body.”

These are among the most important verses in the chapter. The four contrasts describe the transformation between the present body (characterised by Adam) and the resurrection body (characterised by Christ):

1. **Perishable → Imperishable**: No longer subject to decay, disease, or death.
2. **Dishonour → Glory**: The body, buried in humiliation, will share in Christ’s radiant glory.
3. **Weakness → Power**: No fatigue, stress, or limitation.
4. **Natural → Spiritual**: Not “immaterial” (a “spiritual body” still has substance), but fully animated, empowered, and directed by the Holy Spirit, no longer driven by merely natural appetites.

- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-corinthians-15/
- https://www.desiringgod.org/articles/the-overflow-of-easter-a-whole-theology-of-resurrection-in-one-chapter

**Piper (Desiring God):** “Our bodies will be powerful — they will not be subject to stress or fatigue or weakness. Our bodies will be imperishable — they will not get sick, die, age, or become injured. Our bodies will be spiritual — they will be fully oriented to and filled with the Holy Spirit. And our bodies will be glorious” — radiating brightness like the sun (Matt 13:43; Dan 12:3).

- https://www.desiringgod.org/articles/do-we-receive-the-same-body-we-had-on-earth-at-the-resurrection

**Enduring Word (David Guzik, Pentecostal/charismatic):** The resurrection body will be material (like Christ’s) but transformed — no longer subject to corruption, dishonour, weakness, or natural limitation. “Spiritual body” does not mean non-physical; it means a body suited to the spirit and the spiritual realm.

- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-corinthians-15/

---

## v. 45 — “So it is written: ‘The first man Adam became a living being’; the last Adam a life-giving spirit.”

Paul quotes Genesis 2:7. Adam received natural life (*psychē*); Christ, the “last Adam,” gives spiritual life (*pneuma*). By His resurrection, Christ became “a life-giving spirit” — not that He ceased to be human, but that in His glorified state He imparts resurrection life to all who belong to Him.

- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_corinthians/15.htm

---

## vv. 46–49 — “The spiritual, however, was not first, but the natural, and then the spiritual… the first man was of the dust of the earth, the second man from heaven…”

**Traditional reading:** Paul establishes the order of redemptive history: the natural (Adam) came first; the spiritual (Christ) follows. Adam was *ek gēs choikos* (“of the dust of the earth”); Christ is *ex ouranou* (“from heaven”). Just as believers have borne the image of the earthly Adam (by sharing his mortal, fallen nature), so they will bear the image of the heavenly Christ (by sharing His glorified resurrection nature). This is a guarantee rooted in union with Christ.

- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_corinthians/15.htm

---

## v. 50 — “Now I declare to you, brothers, that flesh and blood cannot inherit the kingdom of God, nor does the perishable inherit the imperishable.”

**Traditional reading:** “Flesh and blood” is a Semitic expression for mortal human nature in its present, frail, corruptible state — not a denial of physical resurrection. The point is that our bodies *as they now are* (perishable, sin-affected) cannot enter God’s eternal kingdom. Transformation is necessary.

- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_corinthians/15.htm

Ellicott adds a striking detail: “One characteristic of the resurrection body … is that it shall be bloodless.” Blood was understood as “the type of our lower nature” — e.g., “a man’s blood is up” meaning his physical nature is asserting itself.

- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_corinthians/15.htm

---

## v. 51 — “Listen, I tell you a mystery: We will not all sleep, but we will all be changed—”

**Traditional reading:** “Mystery” (*mystērion*) means something previously hidden now revealed (cf. Rom 11:25; Eph 3:3–5). The mystery is that not all believers will experience death (“sleep”), but all — both the dead in Christ and those alive at His coming — must undergo transformation. The change from the earthly to the spiritual body is “absolutely necessary.”

- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_corinthians/15.htm

**Denominational difference — Dispensational (Baptist/Pentecostal) vs. Reformed/Amillennial:** Dispensational interpreters often link this “last trumpet” (v. 52) with the pre-tribulation rapture (1 Thess 4:16–17) and distinguish it from the seventh trumpet of Revelation. Reformed amillennial and postmillennial interpreters typically identify the “last trumpet” with the final, public return of Christ at the end of history, seeing only one resurrection of believers at Christ’s coming (cf. 1 Cor 15:23: “those who are Christ’s at His coming”). This was not recoverable from the search results for direct quotation from each tradition, but the division is well documented in the wider literature.

---

## v. 52 — “in an instant, in the twinkling of an eye, at the last trumpet. For the trumpet will sound, the dead will be raised imperishable, and we will be changed.”

Ellicott: “The last trumpet is the one which concludes a series which have already been sounding at intervals in notes of warning to the nations (Psalm 47:5; Isaiah 27:13; Jeremiah 51:27).” The trumpet was used to summon an assembly or sound a warning. Paul “states with reiterated emphasis that this change shall not be a protracted process, but a sudden and momentary alteration.”

- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_corinthians/15.htm

**Piper:** Paul “said two things: the dead will be raised (that teaches continuity); and the dead will be changed (they will be made imperishable and immortal).”

- https://www.desiringgod.org/articles/do-we-receive-the-same-body-we-had-on-earth-at-the-resurrection

---

## v. 53 — “For the perishable must be clothed with the imperishable, and the mortal with immortality.”

Ellicott notes that here Paul adds a further thought beyond v. 50: the resurrection body must be suited not only to the *condition* of the new life (spiritual, imperishable) but also to its *duration* — everlasting. The “must” (*dei*) expresses a divine necessity. The imagery of “clothing” (putting on) suggests the body is not discarded but covered over with new qualities — continuity with transformation.

- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_corinthians/15.htm

---

## vv. 54–55 — “Death has been swallowed up in victory … Where, O Death, is your victory? Where, O Death, is your sting?”

**Traditional reading:** Paul conflates Isaiah 25:8 (“He will swallow up death forever”) and Hosea 13:14 in a triumphant taunt. Ellicott notes that in Hosea the original reads “Where is your victory, O death? Where is your sting, O Hades?” — with “Hades” meaning the realm of departed spirits, not the place of torment. Paul’s adaptation changes the rhetorical form but preserves the substance. The Apostle “projects his mind into the future, and, standing in thought with ransomed and raised Humanity after death has been vanquished and the grave been spoiled, he joins in the shout of triumphant praise.”

- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_corinthians/15.htm

---

## v. 56 — “The sting of death is sin, and the power of sin is the law.”

**Traditional reading:** Death is pictured as a venomous creature armed with a sting. Its sting is sin — without sin, death could inflict no real pain (since its penalty would not apply). The “power” (*dynamis*) of sin springs from the law: the law defines sin, exposes it, and even provokes it (cf. Rom 5:12; 7:7–13). The law gives sin its condemning force.

- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_corinthians/15.htm

---

## v. 57 — “But thanks be to God, who gives us the victory through our Lord Jesus Christ!”

**Traditional reading:** Ellicott emphasises that the future victory is so certain Paul speaks of it as a subject for *present* thanksgiving. “The victory is one which God gives now through Jesus Christ. His resurrection is the pledge of our resurrection. His death is the power by which we are enabled to conquer that lower self, from whose crucifixion and death we shall rise to the higher incorruptible life.”

- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_corinthians/15.htm

Gill summarises that the victory over death “is ascribed to God, who gives it through Christ, to whom thanks are returned for it.”

- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-corinthians-15.html

---

## v. 58 — “Therefore, my beloved brothers, be steadfast and immovable. Always excel in the work of the Lord, because you know that your labor in the Lord is not in vain.”

**Traditional reading:** This is the practical conclusion of the entire resurrection chapter. Because the resurrection is certain, Christian life and service have eternal significance. Ellicott: “You might grow weak and faint-hearted if you could think that all your work for God and truth here might be wasted; but it is not so. It cannot be ‘in vain’ if it be ‘in the Lord.’” He adds: “It is very striking and very expressive of the real spirit of the gospel that a chapter which leads us step by step through the calm process of logic, and through glowing passages of resistless eloquence to the sublimest thoughts of immortality, should at last thus close with words of plain and practical duty. Christianity never separates, in precept or in promise, ‘the life that now is’ and ‘that which is to come.’”

- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_corinthians/15.htm
- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_corinthians/15-58.htm

**Gill:** The exhortation is threefold — be “steadfast” in doctrine (especially the resurrection), “unmoveable” in affections and conduct, and “always abounding in the work of the Lord.” The labour of ministers is not in vain because it is “made useful for the conversion of sinners, and the edification of saints, who would be their joy, and crown of rejoicing another day.” For all believers, good works “will follow them; Christ will not forget their work and labour of love.” The doctrine of the resurrection “must be a friend to the practice of good works, as the contrary doctrine must be an obstruction to them.”

- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-corinthians-15.html
- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_corinthians/15-58.htm

**Precept Austin:** “First Corinthians 15:58 is a command issued in light of the marvelous truth associated with the resurrection … Christ has won the battle over sin and death, which should motivate all believers to live with a sure sense of the hope because of Christ’s resurrection from the dead.”

- https://www.preceptaustin.org/1_corinthians_1558_commentary

**Enduring Word (Guzik):** “Death is a defeated enemy because of Jesus; for believers, ‘your labor is not in vain in the Lord’ — knowing we will rise should make us steadfast and immovable in service right now.”

- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-corinthians-15/

**Piper (Desiring God):** “Therefore, do huge amounts of Christ-exalting work because none of it is in vain.”

- https://www.desiringgod.org/articles/the-overflow-of-easter-a-whole-theology-of-resurrection-in-one-chapter

---

## Denominational and Other Distinctives

### Baptist
- **John MacArthur (gty.org)** on vv. 33–34: Emphasises that bad *teaching* (not just bad company) corrupts good morals, tying the Corinthians’ moral failures directly to the heretical denial of the resurrection. Wrong doctrine always produces wrong behaviour. (See v. 33 above.)
- **Gill (studyLight.org):** A classic Particular (Calvinistic) Baptist exposition that stresses divine sovereignty in the resurrection — “God gives it a body as He has designed” — and interprets the “last trumpet” in connection with the final judgment. His entire commentary on the chapter treats the resurrection as the guarantee that “the labour of such who were in the ministry was not in vain.”

### Reformed / Presbyterian
- **Ligonier (ligonier.org):** On v. 33, emphasises the inevitable corrupting influence of bad company, tied to Proverbs 12:26. The Reformed tradition generally sees the “last trumpet” as the final eschatological trumpet at Christ’s return (not a separate rapture event). See also the Desiring God entries above, which represent a broadly Reformed Baptist perspective.

### Pentecostal / Charismatic
- **Enduring Word (David Guzik):** On vv. 42–44, insists the resurrection body is *material* (not ghostly) but transformed — this emphasis on a real, physical, glorified body is characteristic of Pentecostal/charismatic theology, which strongly affirms the goodness of the physical creation and bodily resurrection. Guzik frequently connects the resurrection hope to present-day victorious Christian living and miraculous power.

Catholic teaching (per the *Catechism*) affirms the resurrection of the same body transformed — consistent with the traditional reading above. The Catholic Church also rejects the Mormon interpretation of 1 Cor 15:29 (“baptism for the dead”) as a proof-text for vicarious baptism.
